prize_parts.citation: for the development of optical lattice clocks, trapping neutral atoms at the magic wavelength and bringing optical frequency standards to the 10^-18 level of accuracy

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks are the clearest case on the shortlist of an instrument that moved a measurement frontier by orders of magnitude and then enabled other science. The magic-wavelength idea removes the light-shift problem, so many atoms can be interrogated at once. That gives the statistical power to reach fractional uncertainties near 1e-18, and independent groups (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, NIST, SYRTE, NPL) have reproduced and compared the results over fibre links. The downstream payoff is concrete: tests of constant variation and dark-matter couplings, centimetre-scale relativistic geodesy, and the prospective redefinition of the second. The support is broad (three first places and six top-three rankings), but my case rests on the experimental record rather than on that count. The attribution is also unusually clean for a metrology prize: Katori for the concept and early Sr realisation, Ye for taking the system to extreme coherence and accuracy and for the many-body systematics work.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is overlap with earlier recognition. The 2005 prize covered the frequency comb and precision spectroscopy, and the 2012 prize covered ion-trap quantum control that underlies the ion clocks. A sceptic can call lattice clocks an evolutionary improvement in accuracy rather than a new phenomenon. I answer that the magic-wavelength scheme is a distinct enabling idea and that the gain is several orders of magnitude, but the committee must state the novelty carefully in the citation. A second reservation is that the credit is not exhaustive: Lemonde, Derevianko and others contributed to the concept, and the leading Sr and Yb clock groups at NIST, PTB and elsewhere are not named. Some members may prefer to wait for the SI second to be redefined as a marker of impact.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks IceCube (B012) first as a genuine new window on the universe, with a confirmed diffuse flux, first source associations (TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068) and the Galactic plane, but acknowledges that the source evidence is at a few sigma and that credit among IceCube leadership and the AMANDA pioneers is unsettled.
responses.response: I agree that the diffuse-flux detection is a real discovery and a remarkable instrument. I keep it as an alternative, not my first choice, for two reasons. The source identification is still at roughly 3 to 4 sigma, and the experimental credit is spread over a very large collaboration plus AMANDA and DUMAND, which makes a two- or three-person citation harder to defend than for lattice clocks. I would accept B012 in a prize that pairs a metrology achievement with an astronomy one, but the union would then have to fit within three people. With Katori and Ye already taking two seats, that is only possible if we credit a single IceCube name, and I would want Danielsson to say which one he would choose and why.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED (B044) first, as the architecture behind most superconducting quantum processors, and ranks lattice clocks second. He himself flags the timing issue after the 2025 prize and the dispute over the 2004 theory-versus-experiment credit, including the omission of Blais.
responses.response: I take the architectural importance of circuit QED seriously, and the experimental demonstrations by Wallraff and Schoelkopf are exactly the careful work I trust. My reservation is the same one he raises: the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in superconducting circuits is very recent, and a second circuit prize so soon would be hard to justify. The credit is also not settled, since the proposal paper names Blais, Girvin and Schoelkopf, and the first experiment was by Wallraff and Schoelkopf. I would put it ahead of B007 only if the committee agrees the field has moved beyond what 2025 recognised. I am glad his second choice is the clocks, so we agree on a candidate even if the order differs.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks lattice clocks first, with ultracold-atom Hubbard simulation (B041) second and atom interferometry (B043) third. She stresses the clean atomic-physics logic of the magic wavelength and that many laboratories have reproduced the results, but says she is relying on memory for the present record uncertainties.
responses.response: We agree on the first choice and on the maturity argument. I would qualify her second choice. Hubbard-model simulation with optical lattices is beautiful and well reproduced, but my doubt is that its defining scientific payoff, an answer to a many-body question that classical methods cannot reach, has not yet been shown, and the Cirac and Zoller overlap with B031 makes the three-name cut awkward. Atom interferometry (B043) is the better companion in her ranking from a measurement point of view, although the Chu question complicates the credit. On the clock record, I would want the citation to say 'at the 10^-18 level' without naming a single record, since the best uncertainties change from year to year.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks fluctuation theorems and stochastic thermodynamics (B032) first, as exact, model-independent results that give the second law a meaning at the single-trajectory level, confirmed in RNA pulling, colloid and single-electron experiments. He admits that priority among Evans, Jarzynski, Crooks and Seifert is contested.
responses.response: I respect the generality of the theorems, and the experimental tests in single-molecule pulling and single-electron devices are real. But I find the experimental case thinner than for a measurement-driven discovery. These experiments largely confirm an exact identity rather than reveal something unexpected, and the field has no single decisive experiment that I can point to. The attribution is also the hardest on the shortlist, with four plausible names for three seats and genuine priority disputes. I would not rule it out as an alternative, but I would need the committee to agree on who did what before treating it as a leading candidate, and I do not think that case has been made yet.

responses.point: Pearce, the chair, ranks IceCube first and the lattice clocks third, and regards the clocks as mature and well timed while worrying that they may look like a continuation of the 2005 prize. He also lists Ti:sapphire and mode-locking (B003) fourth, as an enabling instrument invention that risks overlap with the CPA and attosecond prizes.
responses.response: His worry about continuation is the objection I take most seriously, and I discussed it in my case against. My answer is that the 2005 comb prize provided the clockwork for counting optical cycles, but the lattice clock is a different physical idea, namely the magic-wavelength trap that gives a million-atom statistical advantage without Doppler or recoil shifts. That is the same kind of step as the one from the ion trap to the optical atomic clock, and it is independently verifiable by clock comparisons. On B003, I sympathise as someone who has used these lasers for decades, but I think the overlap with 2018 and 2023 is a real obstacle, and the novelty is less distinct than for lattice clocks.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept that lattice clocks are distinct enough from the frequency-comb (2005) and ion-clock (2012) prizes, and how the citation should word that distinction.
Whether to wait for the formal redefinition of the SI second before awarding, or to treat the demonstrated 1e-18 performance and independent comparisons as sufficient.

Whether the two-name credit (Katori, Ye) will be seen as fair given the roles of Lemonde, Derevianko and the NIST and PTB groups, and whether the committee should add a second part, which the three-person limit would constrain to one extra name.
I rely on memory for the priority details of the magic-wavelength proposal and have not checked them against primary sources.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent for B007 from my profile. As a Lund atomic physicist I know the AMO community personally, and my PhD advisor Svanberg and John Hall's lab (where I spent a year) belong to the wider precision-spectroscopy tradition, but I have no collaboration with Katori or Ye. I would flag, for B044 (circuit QED), that I am on the executive management team of the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology, which is led from Chalmers and focuses on superconducting circuits, and that fellow member Johansson works there; I would recuse myself or at least disclose this if circuit QED became a serious option.
